title: Post-Course Portfolio: Online Multiplayer Game Platform
descriptionMarkdown:
# Online Multiplayer Game Platform

## Position in the curriculum

Post-course portfolio, and the hardest entry in the catalog: build this last, after the Real-Time Tic-Tac-Toe or Connect Four/Battleship project (for the core game-session pattern), the Authentication & User Management System (for real accounts), and the Real-Time Chat Application (for authenticated, persisted, room-scoped WebSocket messaging). This project is a generalization of all three, not a fourth unrelated game.

## What is graded, and what is external

This project has a dedicated, automatically-graded checkpoint: **`matchmaking-checkpoint`** ("Fair-pairing matchmaking queue"), a pure in-memory `MatchmakingQueue.run(String input)` program implementing exactly the FIFO pairing, one-queue-membership-at-a-time, and win/loss-record core. Passing its hidden tests proves your matchmaking fairness and results-tracking rules are correct, independent of any real game session or WebSocket transport.

Actually hosting the resulting matches (reusing your earlier game sessions), real-time delivery, and horizontal scaling across multiple server instances are external and self-reviewed.

## Beyond what the lessons taught

This project assumes all the WebSocket and authentication research already done for the earlier real-time catalog entries. Matchmaking queue design and horizontal scaling of stateful WebSocket sessions across multiple server instances are genuinely advanced topics with no single canonical lesson; treat them as open-ended research, and it is entirely acceptable to scope this project to a single server instance (documenting that limitation explicitly) rather than attempting real multi-instance scaling.

## Architecture overview

```text
MatchmakingController/Handler   <- QUEUE/LEAVE requests, matched-notification delivery
MatchmakingService                <- your checkpoint's FIFO-pairing and results rules, reshaped as a Spring bean
GameSession (interface)           <- common abstraction your Tic-Tac-Toe and/or Connect Four logic already implements
PlayerStats (JPA entity)          <- games played/won/lost, updated transactionally at game end
LobbyController                   <- GET /api/lobby, REST listing of currently open/joinable rooms
```

## Build it as vertical slices

1. **Slice 1 — port the checkpoint logic into a service.** Carry your FIFO-pairing, one-queue-at-a-time, and results rules into `MatchmakingService`, unit tests unchanged.
2. **Slice 2 — the common `GameSession` abstraction.** Extract a shared interface your existing Tic-Tac-Toe and/or Connect Four session logic already fits, rather than writing a new game engine.
3. **Slice 3 — hand off a match to a real session.** When the checkpoint's logic reports `MATCHED`, create and start the corresponding `GameSession`, wired to both matched players' connections.
4. **Slice 4 — persisted, transactional statistics.** Update `PlayerStats` for both players atomically when a match ends, for both a normal win and a disconnect/forfeit ending.
5. **Slice 5 — the lobby.** A REST endpoint listing currently joinable/open rooms, which stops listing a room once it is full or completed.

## Common pitfalls

- **Letting a player join two queues, or the same queue twice, concurrently.** The checkpoint's own `QUEUE` contract already rejects this; carry the same one-queue-membership-at-a-time invariant into the real service under real concurrency.
- **Racing two near-simultaneous third/fourth players into the same pair.** Verify, under an actual concurrency test, that a queue reaching exactly two waiting players is matched exactly once, never split across two different matches.
- **Updating statistics non-transactionally, so a mid-update crash leaves one player's record updated and the other's not.** Wrap both players' `PlayerStats` updates in one transaction.
- **Claiming production-grade horizontal scalability without having built or tested it.** State your real scope (documented single-instance, in-memory session state, or whatever you actually built) plainly instead.

## How to self-test what the checkpoint cannot reach

- Fire several near-simultaneous queue-join requests for the same game type and confirm every player ends up in exactly one match.
- End a match by a normal win and, separately, by a simulated disconnect, and confirm both update `PlayerStats` correctly and transactionally.
- Queue players for two different game types at once and confirm each is routed to the correct `GameSession` implementation.

## Required evidence

- A matchmaking concurrency test firing several near-simultaneous join requests and confirming every player is matched into exactly one room, with no player left in two rooms or none.
- A test confirming per-player statistics update transactionally and correctly at game end, including a test of what happens to statistics when a match ends by disconnect/forfeit rather than a normal win.
- A test demonstrating at least two different game types running through the same `GameSession` abstraction, proving the platform layer is genuinely game-agnostic.
- A documented, explicit statement of this project's scaling limitations (single-instance, in-memory session state, or whatever you chose) rather than an implied claim of production-grade horizontal scalability.
- A lobby-listing test confirming a room disappears from the joinable list once it is full or completed.

## Review and completion

A reviewer queues four players for two different game types at nearly the same time, expects two correctly-matched games to start (one per game type, two players each), then has one player in one game disconnect and asks you to demonstrate the documented disconnect policy actually firing, and finally asks you to name, precisely, what would have to change for this platform to run correctly across more than one server instance — an honest answer, not a claim that it already does.
learningObjectives: Complete the graded fair-pairing matchmaking queue checkpoint and carry its verified fairness rules into a real, concurrent matchmaking service
Generalize two or more previously-built game sessions behind one common platform abstraction
Design and test a matchmaking queue's concurrency guarantees under simultaneous join attempts
Update per-player statistics transactionally and correctly for both normal and disconnect-ended matches
State a project's real scaling limitations honestly rather than implying untested production-readiness
